entries.question: Who are you?
entries.answer: I'm Shridhar. I'm the Senior Director of AI and ML at Moderna, where I lead the company's generative AI roadmap. Before that I spent over a decade at Amazon, most recently architecting Alexa's multi-agent conversational framework. I completed my Executive MBA at MIT Sloan, cross-registered at Harvard Business School, this past May.

entries.question: What do you do?
patterns: what do you do for a living
entries.answer: I'm the Senior Director of AI and ML at Moderna, where I lead the generative AI roadmap for more than twenty enterprise applications — conversational agents, function calling, and LLM orchestration for research, manufacturing, and clinical operations. Before Moderna I spent over a decade at Amazon, most recently architecting Alexa's multi-agent conversational systems.

entries.question: What's your background?
patterns: what did you do at amazon
entries.answer: My career started in physics research — I was a fellow at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research working on CERN's GRAPES-3 experiment. From there I moved into distributed systems at Amazon: first building the backend for Amazon's point-of-sale platform, then leading Amazon Retail's launch into Southeast Asia, then years on Alexa leading multi-agent conversational AI and the international launch of Alexa Voice Shopping. Since twenty twenty-three I've been Senior Director of AI and ML at Moderna, running the company's generative AI roadmap. I completed my Executive MBA at MIT Sloan, cross-registered at Harvard Business School, this past May, to pair the engineering side with how to actually run AI as a business.
entries.detail:
Research. Junior Research Fellow at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, working within CERN's GRAPES-3 experimental framework — detector-monitoring algorithms built in C++ and ROOT.

Amazon Register / POS (2012–2015). Software development engineer building distributed services for Amazon Register, the point-of-sale platform — onboarding, payments, and merchant integration systems, with a tech-lead role spanning Seattle and Bangalore.

Amazon Retail, Southeast Asia launch (2015–2018). Manager and tech lead, sole technical owner aligning 26 teams across 7 global orgs to launch Amazon's retail business into Southeast Asia. Cut the standard three-year country launch timeline to nine months, and built the region's first end-to-end digital marketing and last-mile logistics stack, including two-hour delivery in Singapore.

Amazon, Alexa AI and Multimodal Experiences (2018–2023). Senior manager and tech lead for Alexa's conversational AI and multi-agent orchestration, managing 40 direct reports and 145 partner-team engineers across eight-plus countries. Architected and launched Alexa's first multi-agent conversational switching framework — the system behind celebrity personalities like Melissa McCarthy, Shaquille O'Neal, and Amitabh Bachchan, and partner agents like Disney — which underpinned a business generating more than fifty million dollars in annual recurring revenue. Also led Alexa Voice Shopping's international launch across ten markets.

Moderna (2023–present). Senior Director of AI and ML, leading the generative AI roadmap across more than twenty enterprise applications in R&D, manufacturing, and clinical operations, with a team of 35-plus engineers.

Education. Executive MBA, MIT Sloan School of Management, cross-registered at Harvard Business School — completed May 2026. Master's in Computer Science, University of Texas at Dallas (2012). Bachelor's in Computer Science, Pune Institute of Computer Technology (2009).

entries.question: What are you working on right now?
entries.answer: Day to day, I'm leading Moderna's generative AI roadmap. On the side, I'm teaching myself how to build and evaluate multi-agent systems through a personal project I call Noesis, I'm writing a book, and I built a loop engineering system that strips AI-sounding prose out of long-form text — which is also where the voice agent you're talking to right now came from.

entries.question: How do you think about AI?
patterns: how do you think about ai
what do you think about ai
how do you think about evals
entries.answer: The interesting part isn't the model, it's everything around it — how you frame the problem, what context you feed in, and how it fails. The thing I feel most strongly about is evaluation. If your judge and your generator come from the same family of models, agreement between them isn't evidence of anything, because they share blind spots. Self-evaluating loops need at least one grounding signal the models can't talk each other into.

entries.answer: Three habits, and all of them came from getting them wrong first. I run a pilot instead of arguing a design in the abstract, because one country's worth of real numbers ends a debate that a document can't. I align teams on the quality bar before the date, because people will happily agree on a date while holding completely different ideas of what shipping means. And I treat legal and compliance as design partners rather than gates to get past, which is the only reason some of my launches happened at all.

entries.answer: At Moderna I lead AI strategy and engineering for enterprise generative AI. I defined the company's GenAI roadmap across more than twenty enterprise applications — conversational agents, function calling, and LLM orchestration for research, manufacturing, and clinical operations — and I run a cross-functional AI and ML team of more than thirty-five engineers. I've also built partnerships with OpenAI, AWS, and other cloud AI vendors to bring that technology into a regulated pharmaceutical environment.
entries.detail:
Defined and executed Moderna's generative AI roadmap for more than twenty enterprise applications, including conversational agents, function calling, and LLM orchestration workflows across R&D, manufacturing, and clinical operations.

Built and led a cross-functional AI and ML engineering team of more than 35 engineers, delivering production LLM-based applications integrated with AWS and Azure using Python and roughly 30 MLOps pipelines. Architected multi-agent conversational systems using fine-tuning, distillation, and retrieval-augmented generation to automate knowledge work across regulated enterprise workflows, including all of Moderna's document systems.

A good part of the role is translating technical capability into something the business side can act on. I partner directly with the C-suite and business unit leaders to turn AI capabilities into measurable outcomes, and the Executive MBA at MIT Sloan has mattered there — it's given me the language and frameworks to accelerate go-to-market strategy and stakeholder buy-in across pharmaceutical R&D, quality, and regulatory teams. I've also established strategic partnerships with OpenAI, AWS, and other cloud AI vendors to bring current-generation generative AI into the enterprise platform.

I'm building out the pieces of what a real agent orchestration platform needs: policy-as-code and runtime supervision so agent behavior can be monitored and controlled, the orchestration layer itself — tool use, function calling, memory, workflow chaining — and benchmarking models to actually measure whether an agent is reasoning well or just sounding confident.

It's deliberately separate from my Moderna role. The point isn't to build a company; it's to keep my hands on the technical problems underneath agentic AI while my day job increasingly involves strategy and organizational leadership.

entries.question: How did you get training data for ten new markets with none to start?
entries.answer: This was Alexa Voice Shopping's international expansion — ten markets, and voice models need real spoken utterances to train on, so every one of them started at zero. I stopped treating it as a data science problem and treated it as sourcing and logistics. I ran voice collection parties where native speakers recorded real shopping utterances in realistic conditions instead of reading scripts in a booth. I used Amazon's internal employee incentive program to recruit native speakers already inside the company, which gave me a labeled speaker pool at almost no acquisition cost. And where markets shared a language or shopping patterns, I seeded the new model from the closest existing one instead of starting cold. Model iteration went from about eight weeks to three, goal success rate improved by over twenty percent, and all ten markets launched.
entries.detail:
Situation. I was the technical lead and TPM for Alexa Voice Shopping's international expansion — ten markets including India, Japan, Canada, France, Italy, Spain, Mexico, Ireland, and Australia. Voice shopping models need real spoken utterances to train on, and in every new market we had exactly zero. The data science team was small, centralized, and couldn't physically be in ten countries. My launch dates were the thing at risk, so the bottleneck landed on me.

Task. Get each locale enough real training data to hit an acceptable accuracy bar, without a linear headcount increase and without slipping the launch calendar.

Action. I stopped treating it as a data science problem and treated it as a sourcing and logistics problem. Three things:

First, I ran voice collection parties — organized sessions where native speakers in each market recorded real shopping utterances in realistic conditions, rather than reading scripts in a booth. Second, I used Amazon's internal employee incentive program to recruit native speakers already inside the company across our global offices, which gave me a labeled speaker pool at near-zero acquisition cost. Third, I bootstrapped across locales — where markets shared language or shopping patterns, I seeded the new model from the closer existing one instead of starting cold.

Then I wrote it all down. After the first launch I turned the whole sequence into a playbook, and every subsequent locale both used it and improved it.

Result. Model iteration cycles dropped from roughly eight weeks to three. Goal success rate improved by over 20%, and word error rate came down more than 5%. Annotation cost fell because the playbook was reusable and we stood up annotation in lower-cost markets rather than rebuilding a bespoke process per country. All ten markets launched.

entries.question: How did you handle privacy constraints in Japan and the EU?
patterns: how did you work with legal
entries.answer: Japan and the EU were blocked where the other markets weren't — we couldn't route real customer voice data to the labeling and training pipeline, and two of our most important launches were at risk. Rather than ask for an exception to the privacy rules, I designed around them. I built a beta that ran voice isolation on the audio, stripping the identifying information out so what reached the labeling pipeline carried the acoustic and linguistic signal without carrying identity. Getting it approved took many rounds with legal, and the thing that got us to yes was treating them as a design partner rather than a gate. Both markets launched on time.
entries.detail:
Situation. As technical lead for Alexa Voice Shopping's international launch, Japan and the EU markets were blocked on something the other locales weren't: we couldn't route real customer voice data to the labeling and training pipeline. Privacy and regulatory constraints in those markets were stricter, and the data science team had no path to the data they needed. Launch dates for two of our most important markets were at risk.

Task. Find a way to get usable, labeled training data out of these markets without moving personally identifiable information — and get legal comfortable enough to sign off before the launch window closed.

Action. Rather than asking for an exception to the privacy rules, I designed around them. I built a beta program that ran voice isolation on the audio — stripping PII out of the recordings so what reached the labeling pipeline carried the acoustic and linguistic signal the model needed without carrying identity. The beta drew from both opted-in customers and internal employees in those markets, which gave me a mix of real-world usage and a controlled pool I could iterate on quickly.

Getting this approved was not one conversation. I went back and forth with legal repeatedly — each round they'd flag something in the pipeline, I'd change the design, and we'd re-review. I treated legal as a design partner rather than a gate to get past, which is what eventually got us to yes.

Result. Both markets got a compliant training data path and launched with the rest of the program. The isolation-plus-labeling approach became part of the playbook I was building across locales, so later markets with similar constraints didn't restart the legal conversation from scratch.

entries.question: How did you deal with noisy training data in India?
entries.answer: India gave us volume but the quality was poor — wide accent variation, and a lot of audio recorded in real homes with real background noise. I built a two-stage filter: a heuristic pass to drop the clearly unusable, then a human pass over what survived to catch what heuristics can't judge, like a heavily accented utterance that's transcribed correctly. The deliberate choice was not filtering on accent. Accent variation was the thing the model needed to learn, not noise to remove — cleaning it out would have given us a model that worked in a studio and failed in an Indian living room. Word error rate improved by more than five percent and goal success rate by over twenty percent.
entries.detail:
Situation. India was a priority market for Voice Shopping, and the data we were collecting was there in volume but poor in quality. Accent variation across the country was wide, and a lot of the audio came from genuinely noisy environments — real homes with real background noise. The data science team's models were training on it and the accuracy wasn't where it needed to be for launch.

Task. Raise the quality of the training data enough to hit the launch accuracy bar, without throwing away the volume advantage India gave us.

Action. I built a two-stage filter. First, a heuristic pass to catch the clearly unusable — audio where noise dominated signal, or where the transcript obviously didn't match. Then a second human pass over what survived, to catch the cases heuristics can't judge: correct transcription of a heavily accented utterance, or a recording that sounds bad but is actually intelligible and therefore valuable to keep.

The deliberate choice there was not filtering hard on accent. Accent variation was the thing the model needed to learn, not noise to remove — cleaning it out would have produced a model that worked in a studio and failed in an Indian living room. So the filter targeted environmental noise and label errors, and preserved accent diversity.

Result. Word error rate improved by more than 5% and goal success rate by over 20%. And because I stood up the human annotation pass in lower-cost markets rather than building a bespoke expensive process, the annotation cost stayed manageable as we scaled it into other locales through the playbook.

entries.question: How did you get leadership and fifteen teams to agree?
entries.answer: Leadership told me my approach was too complex and there was no way I'd land it inside the launch timeline, and execution depended on more than fifteen groups I didn't own. So I didn't argue the design in the abstract — I ran it in one country first, small enough that nobody had to bet the program on it, and it produced real numbers instead of my opinion. Alongside it I built a date-slip model showing what the calendar looked like if we kept the traditional approach, which changed the question from whether my idea was too complex to which option slips less. With the teams, I learned that aligning on dates alone is useless — people agree to a date while holding completely different bars for what shipping means. So I aligned everyone on model quality bars first, and the schedule negotiation got much simpler.
entries.detail:
Situation. My approach to unblocking the data science team — collection programs, a privacy-safe beta, a two-stage annotation pipeline, all wrapped into a reusable playbook — was not the obvious path. When I took it to leadership, the pushback was that it was too complex and there was no way I'd land it inside the launch timeline. Meanwhile the actual execution depended on 15+ groups I didn't own, spread across regions.

Task. Prove the approach was faster than the skepticism assumed, and then get 15+ independent teams aligned on both a date and a shared definition of "good enough to launch."

Action. I didn't argue the design in the abstract — I ran it in one country first. A single-locale pilot was small enough that nobody had to bet the program on it, and it produced real numbers instead of my opinion.

Alongside it I built a date-slip model: if we kept the traditional approach, here's what the launch calendar actually looks like across ten markets. That reframed the conversation. The question stopped being "is Shridhar's idea too complex" and became "which option slips less."

With the 15+ groups, I learned quickly that aligning on dates alone was useless — teams would agree to a date while holding completely different bars for what shipping meant. So I got them aligned on model quality bars first, then on dates. Once everyone was measuring the same thing, the schedule negotiation got much simpler.

Result. The approach was approved and rolled out across all ten markets. Model iteration went from roughly eight weeks to three. Every locale after the first launched faster than the one before it, because the playbook compounded. The leaders who'd called it too complex ended up with a mechanism the org reused.

entries.question: How did you solve the latency problem in the multi-agent framework?
entries.answer: I was architecting Alexa's first multi-agent conversational framework while also owning the contextual aggregation service, which carried all Alexa traffic — so I was adding a routing hop to the busiest path in the product, and it was costing up to two seconds at p99. In voice there's no spinner, so silence reads as the device being broken. I couldn't remove the work, so I split the response: a hot path that returns immediately with a fast acknowledgment, and a slower path that completes the full multi-agent resolution behind it. The reframe was making time-to-first-byte the metric that mattered instead of time-to-complete. It became the model for how those interactions were handled.
entries.detail:
Situation. I was architecting Alexa's first multi-agent conversational framework — the system that let a user switch between different agents and personalities mid-conversation. I also owned the contextual aggregation service, which carried all Alexa traffic. So I was adding a new routing hop to the busiest path in the product. The framework had to decide which agent owned a given utterance, hand context between personalities, and resolve invocation collisions between agents — and every one of those decisions cost time. We were seeing up to 2 seconds added at p99.

Task. Two seconds is fatal in voice. There's no spinner — silence reads as the device being broken. I had to either get the latency down or change what the user experienced during it, without dropping the framework's capability.

Action. I couldn't remove the work; routing and context handoff genuinely take time. So I split the response.

I designed a hot path that returns immediately with a fast acknowledgment, and a slower path that completes the full multi-agent resolution behind it. The user hears something within the window where silence would have felt broken, and the real answer follows. Time-to-first-byte became the metric that mattered rather than time-to-complete — that's the reframe the whole design rests on.

This hadn't been done in Alexa before. That meant no precedent to point at, and I had to convince people that a fast partial response was better than a slow complete one — which is not obvious to someone looking at a p99 dashboard.

I also made a deliberate call on the routing itself: keep it rule-based and deterministic first, harden it, and only then move toward something more dynamic. Nondeterministic routing on a service carrying all Alexa traffic, on a first-of-its-kind launch, was more risk than the launch could absorb.

Result. The framework launched with the fast-response pattern and it became the model for how these interactions were handled. It supported 8+ voices and multiple agents including partner agents, underpinning a business generating more than fifty million dollars in annual recurring revenue. The Disney launch drove +500 bps engagement in its first month.

entries.question: What was it like shipping the celebrity voices?
entries.answer: Amazon was one of the first companies attempting multi-agent conversational AI at consumer scale and I was leading it — Melissa McCarthy, Shaquille O'Neal, Amitabh Bachchan, then Disney. Huge blast radius, since it touched a service serving all Alexa traffic, and I was briefing senior leadership close to daily. Three things I had to manage at once: talent schedules aren't negotiable, so I sequenced engineering work around the recording calendar rather than the other way around. With leadership I was explicit about what was unknown, which bought credibility for the moments I had to say a date was at risk. And people were genuinely attached to these voices, especially Amitabh Bachchan in India, so I treated subjective quality as a launch gate rather than a nice-to-have. We shipped more than eight voices across Echo and Fire TV in the US and India, on a framework that grew into a business worth more than fifty million dollars a year.
entries.detail:
Situation. Amazon was one of the first companies attempting multi-agent conversational AI at consumer scale, and I was leading it. High-visibility launches — Melissa McCarthy, Shaquille O'Neal, Amitabh Bachchan, then Disney. Enormous blast radius, since it touched a service serving all Alexa traffic, and enormous PR exposure. I was briefing C-suite and senior leadership close to daily. And this was during COVID, when hiring and retaining engineers was as hard as it ever got.

Task. Ship 8+ voices and multiple agents, on schedule, with a team I was struggling to keep staffed, in a technology space with no established playbook.

Action. Three things I had to manage simultaneously.

On the celebrity dependency: talent schedules aren't negotiable and recording windows are narrow. I sequenced engineering work around the recording calendar rather than the other way around, so a missed session couldn't cascade into the launch date.

On leadership: instead of treating daily updates as a tax, I used them. I was explicit about what was unknown, since with brand-new technology the honest answer is often "we don't know yet." That bought credibility for the moments I needed to say a date was at risk.

On the emotional weight: people were genuinely attached to these voices — Amitabh Bachchan in India especially. That raised the quality bar beyond what the metrics captured. A technically-passing voice that felt wrong would have been a failure, so I treated subjective quality as a launch gate, not a nice-to-have.

Result. We launched 8+ voices and multiple agents across Echo and Fire TV in the US and India. Disney drove +500 bps engagement in its first month. Amazon was first to market with multi-agent switching at that scale.

entries.question: What have you built that nobody asked you to build?
patterns: what did you build for yourself
entries.answer: I'm writing a book, and I was using language models in the drafting. The output kept coming back fluent but hollow — the texture that makes prose read as written by a person kept getting sanded off. So I built a loop that chunks the manuscript, scores each chunk for human-likeness, revises, and re-scores until it clears the bar. The interesting part was the scorer, and the interesting part of that was how it failed: the judge and the generator converged. They were both language models, so they shared blind spots — the generator learned to produce text the judge liked and the loop terminated happily on output that wasn't actually good. What fixed it was a set of rules derived from real human writing, a grounding signal from outside the models.
entries.detail:
Situation. I'm writing a book, and I was using LLMs as part of the drafting process. What kept happening was that the output was fluent but hollow — the texture that makes prose read as written by a person kept getting sanded off, plus the usual hallucination problems. I wanted to understand the failure well enough to fix it, so I built a system for it on my own time.

Task. Build something that takes long-form text — novels, books — and iteratively removes AI slop until the writing passes as human, in a way that's actually measurable rather than vibes-based.

Action. I chunked the manuscript and ran each chunk through an iterative loop: score it for human-likeness, revise, re-score, repeat until it clears the bar or the loop gives up.

The interesting problem was the scorer, because "sounds human" is not a metric. I used two things in combination. An LLM-as-judge for the holistic read, and a set of rules derived from actual human writing — patterns pulled from real prose rather than from my intuition about what good writing looks like. The rules matter because the judge alone is too easy to satisfy.

Which is exactly what went wrong. The judge and the generator converged. Because both were language models, they shared blind spots — the generator learned to produce text the judge liked, and the judge kept approving it, and the loop terminated happily on output that wasn't actually good.

That's the thing I'd take to any evaluation problem now: if your judge and your generator come from the same family, agreement between them is not evidence. The rules-from-real-writing layer was what gave me an independent signal — something grounded outside the model's own sense of quality.

Result. Prototype shipped and working. More usefully, it changed how I think about eval design — self-evaluating loops need at least one grounding source the models can't talk each other into.

entries.question: Tell me about a hard call you had to make.
entries.answer: We were hours from launching the celebrity voice product in India with more than fifty press outlets set to cover it, and the contextualization service faltered. We'd set a quality bar of four point seven out of five going in, and launching without that service meant shipping at about four point five. I delayed twelve hours and held the bar. The reasoning was that press coverage is recoverable and first impressions aren't — early adopters in India were the seed population for word of mouth, and you don't get to re-run that. Then I ran a seven-day retrospective and wrote it up properly, and what came out of it went straight into the US celebrity voice launches, which went out with zero downtime.
entries.detail:
Context. We were hours from launching our celebrity voice product in India, with 50+ press outlets set to cover it. We'd set a hard quality bar going in: beta testers scored 4.7 out of 5 on customer satisfaction, and we'd agreed that was the floor, not a target. Then the contextualization service faltered. Launching without it meant shipping at roughly 4.5 — below the bar we'd committed to, in front of the largest audience the product would ever get on day one.

The tension was real on both sides. A 24-hour press cycle doesn't wait; every hour we held was a prime coverage slot lost and revenue exposure taken on. But 4.5 landing on early adopters in a market this visible risked poisoning exactly the network effects the launch existed to create.

Action. I chose to delay by 12 hours and hold the 4.7 bar.

The reasoning was that press coverage is recoverable and first impressions aren't. Early adopters in India were the seed population for word-of-mouth in that market — a soft launch experience from them propagates outward and you don't get to re-run it. Twelve hours of degraded coverage was a cost I could quantify and absorb. A damaged early-adopter cohort was neither.

Result. We launched at the quality bar we'd set. Then I ran a seven-day retrospective on the failure and wrote it up in detail rather than letting the near-miss dissolve once the launch pressure came off.

Learning. The retrospective is the part that mattered. What we found went directly into how we ran the U.S. celebrity voice launches — larger scale, higher stakes — and those went out with zero downtime. The broader lesson I took: a quality bar you'll abandon under launch pressure was never a bar. Setting 4.7 in advance was what made the 12-hour call defensible in the room rather than a judgment call I had to win an argument about.
